stem: Raising the Estimator `resilience_level` from 0 to 2 on real hardware has what expected effect?

options.text: Jobs typically finish faster, because mitigation lets the estimator use fewer shots.
No change in runtime; resilience level only selects which physical qubits are used.
More accurate (less biased) expectation values, at the cost of longer runtime and more QPU usage.
The circuit is automatically simplified to fewer gates before execution.
Expectation values that are typically noisier, because mitigation averages over fewer shots.
The job is rejected unless you also raise `default_shots`, which level 2 generally requires.

explanation.correct: Higher resilience levels build more resilience against errors by running and post-processing larger ensembles of circuits (e.g. ZNE's noise-amplified copies at level 2). This yields more accurate, less biased expectation values but takes longer and consumes more QPU time — a cost/accuracy trade-off.

distractors.A: Mitigation adds overhead (extra circuits and shots), so higher levels are slower, not faster.
distractors.B: Resilience level controls error mitigation, not qubit selection, and it clearly changes runtime.
distractors.D: Gate-count reduction is the transpiler's job (optimization_level); resilience level does not simplify the circuit.
distractors.E: This confuses bias with variance: mitigation adds circuits rather than taking shots away, and the estimator still meets the requested precision — it just spends more QPU time doing so.
distractors.F: Nothing is rejected: the resilience level configures how the estimator spends its budget, and the Estimator sizes its sampling from `precision`, not from a shot count you must raise by hand.

provenance.notes: adversarial s6: hedge added to distractor A (absolute-wording tell) | pool wave: +E mitigation-adds-noise (bias vs variance), +F level-2-requires-manual-shots | realism audit 2026-10-01: stem trimmed; difficulty 3->1 (the documented cost/accuracy trade-off is one recalled fact)
